alalal-e16877-d1e104.summary: Rubric of Article 1: whether the power of sinning is a power or an impotence.

alalal-e16877-d1e117.summary: Lists three questions on the first part: whether the power of sinning is a power or an impotence, whether it is from God, and whether it is one or many.

alalal-e16877-d1e130.summary: First argument for power: rational powers are for opposites (Aristotle); good and evil are opposites, so one power in the rational soul bears on both, and since the power for good is a power, so is the power for evil.

alalal-e16877-d1e149.summary: Second argument: the power of evil is able to do evil, so it is an active power, and every active power is a power, not an impotence.

alalal-e16877-d1e165.summary: Third argument: free choice, defined as the faculty of reason and will by which good is chosen with grace and evil without it, is the power by which evil is done, and will is simply a power.

alalal-e16877-d1e185.summary: Sed contra from Anselm's De libero arbitrio: what diminishes freedom when added and increases it when removed is neither freedom nor part of it; the power of evil diminishes power, faculty and freedom, so it is not a power.

alalal-e16877-d1e210.summary: Second sed contra: if it were simply a power, since God and confirmed angels lack no praiseworthy power, they would have it, which is false.

alalal-e16877-d1e226.summary: Third sed contra: if it were a natural human power, since grace perfects nature and glory grace, it would remain in grace and glory, which is false; so it is a defect and impotence.

alalal-e16877-d1e244.summary: Solution: power for evil is either for pure privative evil, a material defect in all creatures, measured by its minimum, which is not at issue; or power for doing evil, evil as bad action with a deficient and an efficient cause. The latter can be considered in its root in the subject, in its essence, and in its conjunction with act. In the first two respects it is a power, as the Philosopher says the ability to act badly is good. In relation to act, it is a power regarding the substance of the act, a power mixed with impotence regarding the deformed act, and, regarding the deformity alone, not an active power but a material defect and weakness yielding to malice, like the ability to die or be defeated.
claims: The power of sinning is a genuine power in its root and essence, and with respect to the substance of the act.
Regarding the deformity of sin, the power of sinning is not an active power but a defect and weakness.

alalal-e16877-d1e326.summary: This resolves all: the first arguments concern the power in the first, second and third considerations insofar as it relates to the act alone.

alalal-e16877-d1e344.summary: The contrary arguments concern the power as related to defect and deformity. Angels have this power in the first and second senses, though not the third.
claims: Confirmed angels have the root and essence of the power, but not the power as ordered to deformity.

alalal-e16877.summary: Article 1 of Distinction 44 asks whether the power of sinning is a power or an impotence. Arguments for power appeal to rational powers being for opposites, to active power, and to free choice. Against this, Anselm holds that the ability to sin diminishes freedom, and it is absent from God, confirmed angels and the blessed. Albert sets aside the purely material potency to privative evil and analyses the power of doing evil. In its root, in its essence and with respect to the substance of the act, it is a genuine power. With respect to the deformed act it is power mixed with impotence. With respect to the deformity alone it is a defect and weakness yielding to malice, like the ability to die. The arguments on each side hold under different considerations, and angels possess the power only in the first two senses.
claims: The power of sinning is a true power in its root, essence and relation to the substance of the act.
With respect to the deformity of sin, the power of sinning is a defect and weakness, not an active power.
Confirmed angels lack the power of sinning as ordered to deformity.
concepts: substance and deformity of the act
